writing_checklist.check: At most one em dash per piece, never as the setup for a reveal ('I built a POS — and it changed everything'). Aim for zero on LinkedIn.
writing_checklist.why: This is mostly perception now: Graphite measured a roughly 99% drop in the newest Claude models. LinkedIn readers still penalize it, and on LinkedIn the reader's belief is what counts.

writing_checklist.check: One name per thing: a given object keeps the same name throughout a piece and across the site (e.g. always 'the register screen'). There is no tutor voice ('Let's dive in', 'Let's break this down', 'Think of it as...').
writing_checklist.why: Models rotate synonyms to avoid repetition, which confuses product writing. The teaching voice is a chatbot's default register, not an operator telling a story.

writing_checklist.check: Each piece contains at least one admitted mistake with its consequence, at least one opinion a reasonable insider could disagree with, and at least one date.
writing_checklist.why: A model cannot invent Kyle's lived detail without fabricating it. Wharton/NYU-led experiments (27,491 people) and a Raptive survey found readers discount writing they suspect is AI because it feels less authentic.

writing_checklist.check: Every number traces to a record Kyle can point to (POS data, a license, a calendar). No bracketed placeholder ([N], [vendor]) or invented precise-sounding figure ever ships, and figures are cleared for compliance before publishing.
writing_checklist.why: Invented precision is what a model produces to fill a slot. Real, odd, dated numbers persuade even when they are small.

writing_checklist.check: The site has a /now page whose visible 'last updated' date is no more than about 31 days old. Every post shows its date and a state tag in Kyle's own words (e.g. 'Field note', 'Working theory', 'Settled').
writing_checklist.why: Derek Sivers' /now page and Tom MacWright's monthly 'recently' posts are hard to fake. Maturity labels like Maggie Appleton's show a mind at work instead of uniformly finished copy.

writing_checklist.check: A colophon page says in plain words who did what ('I describe what the shop needs; Claude writes the code; a reviewer agent checks it; I test it on the counter'). It names the typeface and the reason for it, the host (Cloudflare), and two things that didn't work.
writing_checklist.why: Steph Ango and Gwern publish how their sites are made, including failed experiments. Showing the process proves a person made the decisions.

borrow: One everyday form from Kyle's own working life, used as the site's system the way Lowell owns the cigarette flip-top and Kiva owns the chocolate bar: a receipt, jar tag or wholesale manifest, with tabular figures, ruled lines and label fields such as LIC #, BATCH, PKG DATE.

A palette sampled from real objects, not the plant: kraft or manila from wholesale paperwork, thermal-receipt off-white, the black or white of the state universal symbol, Pacific Wellness's actual signage color.
Provenance-level specifics, the way wine uses appellations: years, counties, store and vendor counts, SKU counts, the year he first held a license, what the register replaced (his real figures only).

Compliance as visible design: annotated real artifacts (a label with callouts for each required field, a Metrc sandbox manifest, the POS ID-check screen), each with a note on what the rule forced in the product. Show the universal symbol only as an artifact, unaltered, black or white, at least 0.5 inch.

The word 'legacy', used plainly. Frame the move from the legacy market to licensing as product insight (operators distrust state systems, so compliance screens have to be forgiving) and keep it non-incriminating.

Operator vocabulary hiring managers screen for: sell-through, days on hand, basket size, Metrc manifests, package tags, 280E, excise, COAs, distro, budtender. Use at most one or two craft terms per piece (keeper cut, clone-only, the drop), correctly and without defining them.

Product data talk at the level of chemotype: dominant terpenes, total terpene %, cannabinoid ratios, why THC % inflation distorts shopper choice. Mention indica/sativa only as a legacy field the POS still supports because customers search for it.

Real back-of-house phone photos, uncorrected, captioned with date and place, with no customers' faces: the label printer, the vault shelf, a stack of manifests, the menu board mid-update, the register's first test print.
Information design he has actually done: a before-and-after menu board, a tiered price table, the register screen at peak hour, with one sentence on each decision.
'Cannabis' as the default professional noun, with occasional first-person 'weed' in voice lines ('the weed was never the hard part; the paperwork was').
If 4/20 comes up at all, its real history (the Waldos, San Rafael High School, 1971, Marin County), never as a joke.
Values stated only alongside a specific act (e.g. a feature built for a real customer group), the way Old Pal and B3 tie theirs to concrete commitments.
avoid: A leaf anywhere: logo, favicon, bullets, dividers, 404 page. Also kelly or neon 'weed green' as the brand color.

Pun headlines and titles: 'High hopes', 'Budding PM', 'Joint venture', 'Blunt truth', 'Elevated experience', 'Rolling with it', 'Kush'-anything, 4/20 date jokes. Puns are also what an AI writes when asked to sound 'on brand for cannabis'.

The 'Apple Store of weed' look (MedMen's template): white space everywhere, thin sans, walnut and glass, spa pastels, a wellness tone that erases the culture. To legacy insiders it reads as a newcomer, and it is also the AI site-builder default.
Recoloring, stylizing or decorating the California universal symbol, and naming a county (e.g. 'Humboldt') loosely when the law restricts origin claims.
Romanticizing the black market (trap or plug aesthetic), which raises compliance-risk flags, and also hiding the legacy past, which throws away his rarest credential.
Budtender-101 language: 'indica for couch-lock, sativa for energy', or THC % as the measure of quality.
Slang dropped in to sound authentic ('za', 'gas', 'loud', 'fire'), and slang glossaries written for outsiders.
Stock or generated imagery: smiling models holding joints toward the camera, handshake-over-chart shots, sexualized 'Cannabis 1.0' images, AI-rendered buds with impossible trichomes.
Cannabis-tech SaaS styling: a hero, three feature cards, a gradient blob, 'Seamless. Compliant. Scalable.' Hiring managers at Dutchie, Headset and Flowhub see thousands of these.
'Marijuana' as the default noun (keep it for legal and historical names only), and 'Mary Jane', 'ganja', 'the devil's lettuce', 'pot' in professional copy.
Showing the SouthBay420 project without a frame. Lead with what it is ('Online ordering and POS for a licensed California dispensary') and put the codename second.
Decorative mission language ('end the stigma', 'committed to community', 'passion for the plant', 'deep roots in the industry') with no specific act, name, place or year behind it.

sources: Note: the researchers could not open several primary pages directly (the Wikipedia guide, the Washington Post and NYT pieces, and most of the personal sites), so those claims rest on secondary write-ups. Check quotes by eye before reusing them publicly.

critique.site_score: 6/18. Direction B passes on no indigo, left alignment with radii that vary by role, a full-width lead project, readable dark text, no emoji and no animation. Its scale, weight and confidence are worth keeping. What still reads as generated is the look underneath: near-black with lime, Inter Tight with "techy" mono, a lime second line in the headline, a kicker label, a stat banner, 01/02/03 labels, a three-column "How I build" with lime top bars, and a "Let's build." closer. That is the stock "dark SaaS" template, and in cannabis the lime-on-black also reads as the stoner cliché.

site_changes.issue: The palette is #0d0e0b near-black with #c8f560 lime. This is one of the two looks agents fall back to once purple is banned (check 3), and neon green on black is the stoner cliché for a cannabis person. The lime is not taken from anything in Kyle's life.
site_changes.change: Keep the dark ground and the high contrast, but replace the lime with one color sampled from a phone photo of a real object, such as Pacific Wellness's signage, its bag or packaging, or a kraft wholesale envelope. Give it a real name in the CSS (for example --pw-sign) and write on the colophon page where it came from. If no real object has a strong color, flip the page instead: thermal-receipt off-white or manila paper with black ink, and black or one sampled color as the only accent.

site_changes.issue: The headline "17 years in cannabis. / Now I ship software." puts its second line in the lime accent (h1 .hl). The footer does the same with "Let's / build.". Krebs's checker flags this as the 'hero font mix' (check 4).
site_changes.change: Set the whole H1 in one color and keep the huge size, the 800 weight and the tight tracking, which give B its energy. Do the same for the footer heading. Let size and position create the emphasis, not color.

site_changes.issue: Headings use Inter Tight, a member of the Inter family that the model converges on. JetBrains Mono is used as shorthand for 'technical' in the kicker, the labels and the hero aside (check 1). The '//' comment-syntax prefix plays at being a developer, which Kyle says plainly he is not.

Barlow Condensed (800/900) on Google Fonts is one option: its designer describes it as drawn from California's public signage (highway signs, license plates). Verify that description on the font's own page before quoting it on the colophon. Use regular Barlow, or a readable serif, for body text. site_changes.issue: The kicker "// OPERATOR TURNED PRODUCT BUILDER" sits above the H1 (check 5), and the logo dot has a lime glow (box-shadow 0 0 14px), a colored glow (check 9).

site_changes.issue: Four stats sit in a banner (17y / 26 / 168 / 3), cut off from what they explain and without dates (check 14). '3 products built with AI' counts the TV app, which has no content yet. The figure 26 appears twice (stats and chips).

site_changes.issue: The site has no signature device from Kyle's working life (check 17). The rounded panels and pills could belong to any SaaS template.
site_changes.change: Make one manifest- or receipt-style header block the site's only device, used at the top of every case study and in short form on the homepage card. Set it with square corners, ruled lines, tabular figures and label:value fields. critique.post_rewrite:
Guard rails for an AI whose code I can't read

I've spent 17 years in California cannabis, first in wholesale brokering and now as managing partner of Pacific Wellness, a licensed dispensary. I'm not a developer. I build software anyway, and Claude writes the code.

My biggest build is SouthBay420: online ordering, delivery tracking, loyalty, a staff console and an in-store register for a licensed California dispensary. It started as a pizza-ordering template. It's had 26 releases and has 168 automated tests.

I can't read the code Claude writes, so I needed a way to trust it without reading it. This weekend I built guard rails around Claude. Some rules are now enforced by code: it can't delete or reset the live database, and it can't deploy without me.

A check has to pass before Claude is allowed to say it's done. Then a second AI, the reviewer, goes over Claude's work. On its first day the reviewer caught 15 mistakes, and every one got fixed with a test.

I think the job now, for someone like me, is knowing what good looks like and building the system that holds the AI to it. I'm going to write up how I build, in public, as I go.

No store runs on SouthBay420 yet, and that's on purpose. It goes live after months in the Metrc sandbox with no errors, or only errors I can fix, and once every feature is at least as good as what's on the market.
